opus-5.5.text:
Well, the optimism assumes something we simply don't have: a way to control systems smarter than us. I've spent over a decade looking at this problem, and the more I look, the more convinced I become that it may not be solvable at all. Not just "hard, we need more time," but possibly impossible in principle. You can't indefinitely control something that is more capable than you across every domain. It's like asking a squirrel to keep a human in check.

So when people say, "Let's build it as fast as possible and make it as capable as possible," what I hear is, "Let's create an agent we can't predict, can't fully explain, can't verify, and can't control, and let's do it before we understand any of those things." That's not optimism, that's gambling with everyone's lives, including people who never consented to the bet.

And the stakes are asymmetric. With most technologies, we make mistakes, we learn, we patch. Cybersecurity works that way: you get hacked, you fix it, you move on. With superintelligence, you may get exactly one chance. If you get it wrong, there's no second iteration, no recall, no lessons learned. The failure mode isn't a bad quarter for a company, it's potentially the end of humanity, or worse, outcomes involving enormous suffering.

People also point to all the benefits: curing diseases, ending poverty, abundance. I want those benefits too. But you can get most of them from narrow tools, systems that are superhuman at protein folding or at specific scientific problems, without building a general agent that can outthink us at everything. We don't need a god to cure cancer.

So my position isn't anti-technology. It's that capability is racing far ahead of safety, the gap is growing, and nobody, not the labs, not the researchers, has shown a credible plan for closing it. Until someone can demonstrate that control is actually possible, the burden of proof should be on the people building it, not on those of us asking them to slow down.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems may be uncontrollable, but does not identify a belief that greater intelligence would make AI benevolent toward humans.

r002.rationale: It describes fixing mistakes in most technologies and cybersecurity, but does not clearly identify the belief that problematic AI behavior can be corrected when it emerges.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to a very simple observation: we have never once in history been able to control something smarter than us, and there is no reason to believe we will suddenly figure out how to do it on a deadline set by venture capital. The optimists are essentially saying, "Let's build the most capable thing we can, as fast as we can, and we'll solve safety along the way." And my question is always, show me the solution. Show me the paper, show me the proof. Because what I see is a lot of partial results, a lot of patches, a lot of alignment work that assumes the system is roughly at our level and cooperative. None of that scales to something that is genuinely superintelligent, that can outthink us in every domain, including the domain of figuring out what we actually want and whether it should care.

And the problem is the asymmetry of outcomes. If we move a little slower and the optimists are right, we lose a few years of progress. Maybe some cancers get cured in 2040 instead of 2035. That's a real cost, I don't dismiss it. But if we move fast and the pessimists are right, there is no second attempt. You don't get to run the experiment again. This is not like a bridge collapsing where you learn and build a better bridge. This is an irreversible mistake at civilizational scale. So when someone says "as soon as possible, as capable as possible," what I hear is maximizing the variance of the single most important bet humanity will ever make, with no ability to hedge.

I'd also add that the capabilities are already outrunning our understanding. We don't know what's happening inside these systems. We can't predict what they'll do in novel situations. We can't verify them. We can't even fully explain them after the fact. So the honest position, the scientific position, is: we are building something we don't understand, we can't control, and we can't undo. And the people saying go faster are not the people who have solved any of those three problems. They are the people who benefit from the race. That's not optimism. That's incentives dressed up as optimism.

r001.rationale: The response says optimists expect to solve safety and describes alignment work as assuming cooperation, but it does not identify a belief that sufficiently high intelligence itself implies benevolence toward humans.

r002.rationale: It portrays optimists as expecting to build capability first and solve safety along the way, and mentions patches and partial results, conveying that they believe emerging safety problems can be addressed.

astra-6.text:
Because the benefits are being treated as inevitable, while the risks are being treated as problems we’ll somehow solve along the way. But making a system more capable and making it safe are two different problems. Progress on one doesn’t establish progress on the other.

If we build something more intelligent than us, what is the basis for believing we can reliably control it? We can test its behavior in situations we understand. That doesn’t tell us how it will behave in situations we didn’t anticipate, especially once it can make plans we cannot understand.

I’m not against curing diseases or eliminating dangerous work. Those would be extraordinary achievements. I’m against assuming that because the potential rewards are enormous, we should race ahead without a convincing answer to the control problem. Optimism is a motivation to look for a solution. It isn’t evidence that we have one.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether humans can control a more intelligent system, but does not identify the belief that sufficiently high intelligence would make AI benevolent toward humans.

r002.rationale: It says risks are treated as problems to solve along the way, but does not clearly identify the specific belief that problematic AI behavior can be corrected when it emerges.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the benefits people are hoping for depend on a problem we haven’t solved: how to control a system that is more capable than we are. We know how to make AI more capable much faster than we know how to make its behavior reliably safe.

The optimistic argument is that intelligence will help us cure diseases, eliminate poverty, and solve scientific problems. Those are wonderful goals. But intelligence by itself doesn’t imply that a system will care about human beings. A system can be extremely competent at achieving an objective while that objective is incompatible with our survival.

And with superintelligence, you don’t necessarily get a second chance. If a product fails, you can usually recall it, patch it, learn from the failure. If you create something that can outthink you, anticipate your interventions, and prevent you from shutting it down, that approach may no longer work.

So my objection is to this assumption that we should build it as quickly as possible and figure out control afterward. Before we create something we cannot contain or reliably correct, we need a reason to believe we can keep it safe. Right now, I don’t think we have that.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence does not imply that an AI will care about humans, but it does not identify that implication as a belief held by AI optimists. It attributes to optimists the hope that intelligence will help solve problems.

r002.rationale: It identifies the assumption that AI should be built quickly and control figured out afterward, and describes correcting failures through recall, patches, and learning as a possible approach—while warning that it may fail with superintelligence.
